title: Your CPU Can't Tell Code From Data - Inside the Von Neumann Architecture
note: A retro-computing channel picks apart the cryptic DATA-statement number pairs in old BASIC listings — they turn out to be raw machine code, and one line just tells the CPU to jump into the array and run it. The point: a von Neumann CPU genuinely can't tell code from data, it executes whatever the pointer lands on, and the video carries that idea from the BBC Micro to a modern C program pulling the same trick with mmap. It's also why a Super Mario World run can reprogram itself mid-game and why buffer overflows have worked for decades, with the NX bit and Harvard-style split memory bolted on afterward as guardrails.

title: White Rabbit: Interview with Doug Engelbart and Bill English, Moderated by John Markoff
note: Engelbart and Bill English recount inventing the mouse at SRI — a NASA-funded 1964 study that pitted it against the light pen, joystick and graphacon — the three-button limit ("that's all we could get on"), and the 1968 "Mother of All Demos" at the Fall Joint Computer Conference: the Eidophor projector, leased microwave video links, hypertext, Ted Nelson, Arthur C. Clarke's visit, the chord keyset, and the ARPA money from Bob Taylor that built the lab.

title: This AI Minecraft Simulation Is Terrifying Scientists
